slot.brief: Give E°cell (and n) for a reaction and compute ΔG°; alternatively use ΔG° = −nFE° = −RT ln K to find the equilibrium constant sign or magnitude for the given cell.

stem:
For the cell reaction:
$$\text{Cd}(s) + 2\text{Ag}^+(aq) \rightarrow \text{Cd}^{2+}(aq) + 2\text{Ag}(s)$$
the standard cell potential is $E^\circ_\text{cell} = +1.20\ \text{V}$ at $298\ \text{K}$. The standard Gibbs energy change ($\Delta G^\circ$) for the reaction is:
(Take $1\ \text{F} = 96500\ \text{C mol}^{-1}$)

verdicts.working: n = 2 electrons (Cd → Cd²⁺). ΔG° = −nFE°cell = −2 × 96500 × 1.20 = −231600 J mol⁻¹ = −231.6 kJ mol⁻¹.

working:
The two half-reactions are:
Anode (oxidation): $\text{Cd}(s) \rightarrow \text{Cd}^{2+}(aq) + 2e^-$
Cathode (reduction): $2\text{Ag}^+(aq) + 2e^- \rightarrow 2\text{Ag}(s)$

Thus, the number of moles of electrons transferred in the balanced cell reaction is $n = 2$.

The relation between standard Gibbs energy change and standard cell potential is:
$$\Delta G^\circ = -nFE^\circ_\text{cell}$$

Substitute the given values:
$$\Delta G^\circ = -2 \times 96500\ \text{C mol}^{-1} \times 1.20\ \text{V}$$
$$\Delta G^\circ = -231600\ \text{J mol}^{-1} = -231.6\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$$

Independent check: n = 2 electrons (Cd → Cd²⁺). ΔG° = −nFE°cell = −2 × 96500 × 1.20 = −231600 J mol⁻¹ = −231.6 kJ mol⁻¹.

Option C encodes using $n = 1$ along with a sign error (omitting the minus sign in $\Delta G^\circ = -nFE^\circ$).
